account: RL-Zero's weight change (0.24 % of the weight norm) is concentrated in 8 input-output pairs per matrix, as in every on-policy RL run whatever the reward (top-8 share 0.12-0.21, LM-judge General 0.127, against 0.03 for imitation-trained Think-SFT); the input side of each pair is set by the base's own activations on any step-by-step text (driven 8-11x a random subspace, code text 0.87 as much as math), which is why Think-SFT's and Code-RL's changes also land there and Math's per-matrix pattern follows Think-SFT's (rho 0.59), not IF-RL's (-0.01); the output side, the pairing, is what the reward chose (shifted pairs or random outputs do nothing, and the base's later layers enlarge only the real pairs, 95x a random edit).

The pairs act in every sample as a graded shift of the base's own choices, not as an on/off switch of a mode: direction 1 and layers 22-31 mostly set when the answer stops, while directions 2-8 in layers 0-21 re-rank which route the answer takes in its first half toward routes the base already writes at a low rate (on hard328 problems the cued base never solves in 4, a fresh base sample is right 5 %, RL 15 %, the 1.5x edit 14 %).

The base fails in two ways: chance slips, after which it is as likely to finish right as from the start and whose wrong answers split (same-problem agreement 0.26), and early route errors (a misreading has already cost 32 points before its sentence), and RL's advantage is in the text by the halfway point.

Inference reaches what is one early choice or a chance event: a three-token cue, a self-chosen 'Okay' opening or a one-tensor hand edit fixes the opening (397-411 of 500, the level of RL step 100 with its cap-hit rate and +7-point vote gain), and a plurality vote over 4-12 samples at T 1.0 (not T 0.6, where 52-63 % of long answers loop, and not under a 4,096 cap) removes slips wherever the right route is already the base's plurality (81 % of the MATH-500 gap lies where the base solves at least 1 of 4; a vote over 6 equals one RL sample).

No prompt, sampling rule or vote re-ranks routes after the opening, so where the right route is rare and the wrong answers split the base stays short (no right sample on 26 of the 36 hard328 problems RL's vote wins; vote 8.8 points under RL), while the 1.5x edit, whose extra half stands in for the diffuse 88 % left out (not a bf16 loss: 0.99996 of the intended change is written), carries the re-ranking and matches RL per sample, under the vote and past the base's reach (456 vs 457; 200.25 vs 200.0; vote 216.25 vs 215.92; 0.88 of RL's lift).

Because the shift is graded and present in every sample, an edited or partly trained model's answer that skips the deliberative opening still carries it (short 1x-edit answers are 82.9 % right, m21's quick wrong answers are not answer-first replies), so the cue adds little once the weights have moved (+8.5 of 500 at step 100), and an edit made of RL's top pairs alone carries RL's gains but not the losses that sit in the rest of the change (where RL-Code fails base-passed problems the Code edit passes at the base's resample rate, 0.45 vs 0.44).

denials.why: Account-1's S2/S4 reading, that a step-100 plain sample which does not open deliberatively is an unswitched plain-base answer, is wrong: after 100 RL steps the weights carry a graded shift in every sample, so how a sample opens says little about whether it is right. The cue's +8.5 of 500 is spread thinly over samples, not concentrated in a few base-like ones.
denials.instead: Sentence 6 (the shift is graded and present in every sample): on the same problems the step-100 cue samples beat the non-deliberative plain samples by little, D1 in [-0.10, 0.12].

denials.why: The premise that m21's non-deliberative answers are plain-base answers (about 0.35-0.5 right) is wrong. Code's pairs at 1x shift every sample by a graded amount: short 1x-edit answers are 82.9 % right, m21's quick wrong answers are not answer-first replies, and S = 0.414 sits above the lottery range. So on problems the cued base solves, m21's non-deliberative answers are right nearly as often as its deliberative ones.
denials.instead: Sentence 6: the gap between m21's deliberative and non-deliberative answers on cued-solved problems is small, G in [-0.10, 0.17].

consequences.claim: Sentence 1 says the input side of RL's pairs is fixed by the base's activations, so any training on step-by-step text lands there, while the output side is chosen by the reward. Think-SFT (imitation) should therefore sit in Math 3.1's top-8 subspace much less on the output side than on the input side, relative to Math 3.0, which has the same reward and shares both sides. Diffuseness alone gives a ratio of 1, because the chance levels cancel.
consequences.why_new: F27 and F46 (results 3abd6f and 105d5c) used cap_right (input side) only. No fact or result reports the output-side capture (cap_left) of Think-SFT or Math 3.0, or the two sides set against each other.
consequences.statistic: Q = median over matrices of [cap_left(Think-SFT, Math 3.1 top-8) / cap_right(Think-SFT, Math 3.1 top-8)] / [cap_left(Math 3.0, Math 3.1 top-8) / cap_right(Math 3.0, Math 3.1 top-8)], unitless
consequences.rows: All 224 layer matrices (32 layers x q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) with cap_left and cap_right for both Think-SFT and Math 3.0 against the Math 3.1 top-8 subspace entry (left singular vectors for cap_left, right for cap_right)
consequences.computation: 1) Per matrix read the four capture shares. 2) r_TS = cap_left_TS / cap_right_TS and r_M30 = cap_left_M30 / cap_right_M30; the rank-8 chance levels (8/d_out and 8/d_in) are the same for both models, so they cancel in q = r_TS / r_M30. 3) Q = median of q over the 224 matrices. 4) Bootstrap: resample matrices with replacement 10,000 times, recompute the median; the 90 % interval is the 5th-95th percentile. 5) Also report Q with Code 3.1 in place of Think-SFT, as a description only.
consequences.null: Another model's directions: whatever lands in Math 3.1's top-8 subspace lands there alike on both sides, whatever the objective. Think-SFT's output/input ratio then equals Math 3.0's (Q about 1), which is also the value pure diffuseness gives.

consequences.claim: Sentences 2 and 5 say the 1.5x edit carries RL's re-ranking of routes, not just fewer slips. So where both fail, the edit's wrong answers should be closer to RL's than the base's are. The agreement is normalized by each model's own wrong-answer concentration, so a model that is merely sharper does not score higher. If the edit only lowered slips (account-1), its wrong answers would be drawn like the base's and the difference would be about 0.
consequences.why_new: F45, F48 and result-064aac measured agreement among the cued base's own wrong answers only, and F50, F52 and F53 compared right rates. No fact or result compares wrong answers across the edit, RL and the base.
consequences.statistic: D = N(E,R) - N(B,R), with N(X,R) = A(X,R) / sqrt(A(X,X) * A(R,R)). A(X,Y) is the pooled share of same-problem pairs of finished wrong answers that agree (cross pairs between two models, within pairs for one model); E = base + 1.5x top-8, R = RL plain, B = cued base. Unitless.
consequences.rows: hard328 problems where each of E, R and B has at least 1 finished wrong answer (v3 wrong, not a cap hit, an extracted answer present) among attempt-0 samples 0-3; within-model pairs from the problems among these where the model has at least 2
consequences.computation: 1) Per model and problem, list the extracted answers of the finished wrong attempt-0 samples 0-3; two answers agree when math-verify 0.9.0 judges them equal. 2) Keep the problems in rows. 3) A(E,R) and A(B,R) = agreeing cross pairs / all cross pairs, pooled over the problems; A(E,E), A(B,B), A(R,R) = agreeing within pairs / within pairs, pooled. 4) D = N(E,R) - N(B,R). 5) Bootstrap: resample problems with replacement 10,000 times and recompute all five A's and D; the 90 % interval is the 5th-95th percentile. 6) Null value: the same D with E replaced by the base's samples 2-3 and B by the base's samples 0-1 (both against RL), with the same bootstrap. Report undecided if fewer than 50 problems qualify.
consequences.null: The base's own resample: the edit's wrong answers are drawn like the base's (the edit only lowers the slip rate), computed as the base's samples 2-3 against its samples 0-1, each against RL. This gives D about 0.

consequences.claim: The same consequence of sentences 2 and 5 on 136 contest problems published in 2026, after all weights existed. The edit shares RL's route re-ranking, so where all three fail its wrong answers are closer to RL's than the cued base's are, after normalizing for each model's own wrong-answer concentration.
consequences.why_new: result-04e329 and the fresh readouts report right counts only. No fact or result compares wrong answers across models on fresh2026.
consequences.statistic: D_fresh = N(E,R) - N(B,R) on fresh2026, defined as in c2. Unitless.
consequences.rows: fresh2026 problems where each of the edit (base + 1.5x top-8, cue), RL plain and the cued base has at least 1 finished wrong answer (v3) among its 4 samples; within pairs from the problems where the model has at least 2
consequences.computation: As in c2, steps 1-6, on the fresh2026 rows of the three run folders: math-verify equality of extracted answers, pooled cross and within agreement shares, D = N(E,R) - N(B,R), 10,000 bootstrap resamples over problems, 90 % interval = 5th-95th percentile. Null value: the base's samples 2-3 against its samples 0-1, each against RL. Report undecided if fewer than 50 problems qualify.
consequences.null: The base's own resample: the edit's wrong answers are drawn like the cued base's, so D is about 0 (base samples 2-3 against base samples 0-1, each against RL).

cell.why: Sentences 4-5: inference can fix only the opening choice; an opening that asks the base to restate the problem does not re-rank the routes it takes afterwards. So the score stays at the cued base's level on these problems (158.5 of 328 per sample, about 0.48, so about 79-80 of 164) and well under RL (about 100 of 164).
